slides.title: Step 2: *Context*
slides.text: What does the model get to see?

narration: Step two is about what an AI model gets to see.
Everything the model can see when it answers is called its context.
To get there, documents are cut up, turned into numbers, stored and searched.
In our own measurements, these choices changed the answer more than anything else.

slides.caption: Step two decides what reaches the model. How documents are cut up, turned into numbers, stored and searched changes the answer.

slides.title: What we will *cover*
items: When a document covers many topics

narration: Some changes to an AI system are worth trying before others.
The first three are tried in order, one step at a time.
This order is called the ladder.
Step one was the instructions you give the model.
This is step two, context.
First, we follow a document on its way to the model.
Then we see what goes wrong when one document covers many topics.
We also see how to test a fix fairly.
After that, we look at searching for exact details.
Then we look at who chooses and owns the documents.
Last, we look at what is kept for later use.
The video ends with the test for moving on.

slides.caption: Step two of the ladder is context. This video follows a document to the model. It then covers exact search, looking after documents and what is kept.

slides.title: A document passes through *five stages*

narration: A system that uses a model to do a job is called an agent.
To answer questions, an agent often needs facts from documents.
Let us follow one document on its way to the model.
First, the file is read and turned into text.
Then the text is cut into smaller pieces.
Each piece is turned into a list of numbers.
The numbers are stored so they can be searched quickly.
Then a question comes in.
The best pieces are found and passed to the model.
Each stage has its own name.
We will take them one at a time.

slides.caption: A document is read, cut into pieces, turned into numbers, stored and searched. The best pieces reach the model.

slides.title: Turn the file into *text*
slides.text: A lost structure cannot be fixed later.

narration: The first stage turns the file into plain text.
This is called parsing.
Good parsing keeps the structure, like the rows and columns of a table.
Say a table is flattened into one long sentence.
The numbers lose the labels that went with them.
No later stage can put that back.
So keep checking samples of the parsing.

slides.caption: Parsing turns a file into text and keeps its structure. A table flattened into a sentence loses which number goes with which label. No later stage recovers it.
slides.picture: A neat table on a sheet beside the same boxes squashed into one long broken strip.

slides.title: Cut the text into *pieces*
slides.text: Pieces must be neither too large nor too small.

narration: The second stage cuts the text into pieces that search can find.
These pieces are called chunks.
A chunk that is too large mixes several topics.
A chunk that is too small loses the text around it.
Without that text, it can lose its meaning.
No single size works for every set of documents.
So the size has to be tested.

slides.caption: Chunking splits text into pieces search can find. Too large and a piece covers several topics. Too small and it loses its meaning. The size is tested.
slides.picture: A very large sheet, a tiny scrap and one medium piece of paper that is the right size.

slides.title: Turn each piece into *numbers*
slides.text: Pieces with similar meaning get similar numbers.

narration: The third stage turns each piece into a list of numbers.
The numbers stand for what the piece means.
This list of numbers is called a vector.
Think of each vector as a point on a map of meaning.
Pieces that mean similar things sit close together.
Pieces about different things sit far apart.

slides.caption: Each piece becomes a vector, a list of numbers. Pieces that mean similar things end up close together.
slides.picture: Three paper pieces each become a dot, and the two with similar meaning sit close together.

slides.title: Store the numbers for *search*
slides.text: The store also records who may see each document.

narration: The fourth stage stores the vectors so they can be searched fast.
This store is called an index.
The index also records who is allowed to see each document.
The search uses that record later.

slides.caption: The index stores the vectors for fast search. It also stores who may see each source.
slides.picture: A long drawer of neatly filed cards with divider tabs, and one card lifted out.

slides.title: Find the *nearest* pieces
slides.text: Only the closest pieces reach the model.

narration: The last stage starts when someone asks a question.
The question is turned into a vector in the same way.
The search finds the pieces whose vectors sit nearest to it.
Those pieces are passed to the model along with the question.
Finding and passing on the right pieces is called retrieval.

slides.caption: Retrieval turns the question into a vector, finds the nearest pieces and passes them to the model.
slides.picture: A question card draws the three nearest paper pieces out of a scatter and hands them to a small model device.

slides.title: Filter by permission *before* the search

right.head: Filter before
rows: Search only what you may see

narration: Retrieval needs one more rule.
Not everyone is allowed to see every document.
One way is to search everything first.
Then remove what the person may not see.
The other way narrows the search first.
It only searches what that person is allowed to see.
Filtering afterwards leaks information.
Even the number of results can show that a hidden document exists.
Filtering first gives no such hint.

slides.caption: The index stores who may see each source. The search is narrowed to what the person asking may see. Filtering afterwards leaks what exists.

slides.title: One vector for a document is an *average*
slides.picture: A folder split into four sections, each pulling on a single dot that ends up stuck in the middle, near none of them.
items: A weak match for each topic

narration: Now to a mistake that catches almost everyone.
Say a whole document gets just one vector.
That vector is roughly the average of everything in the document.
That is fine if the document is about one thing.
But documents at work are rarely about one thing.
Picture a long document that covers four different topics.
Its one vector sits in the middle of all four.
It is close to none of them.
Now ask about just one of those topics.
The document comes back as only a weak match.

slides.caption: A document about one thing is fine. Documents at work rarely are. A question about one topic then matches the averaged vector only weakly.

slides.title: We *measured* it
slides.text: Same documents, same model, only the vectors changed.

narration: We tested this in our own experiments.
We made each document cover more topics, from one up to ten.
Everything else stayed the same.
Search quality fell sharply.
Then we gave each document several vectors instead of one.
That brought search quality almost all the way back.
We repeated this on two different machines.
The result was the same.

slides.caption: Our own test, with documents, model and scoring held fixed. Quality fell as topics grew. Several vectors per document recovered almost all of it.
slides.picture: A folder with four sections, each joined to its own dot, and a question card joined to the one dot it needs.

slides.title: More vectors also mean more *chances*
slides.text: Compare with the same number of plain pieces.

narration: There was a problem with that result.
Several vectors give a document more chances to match a question.
So some of the gain might come just from having more pieces.
We ran a fairer test to check.
We shaped pieces around what each part of a document was for.
We compared them with the same number of plain chunks.
On real text, our shaped pieces did worse.

slides.caption: On real text, pieces shaped around a purpose scored below plain chunks with the same number of pieces. More pieces alone can look like a better design.
slides.picture: Many darts around a target, most off centre, and one in the middle.

slides.title: Beat a *matched control* first
slides.text: Same number of pieces, on your own questions.

narration: So test any new design against a plain version.
Give the plain version the same number of pieces.
A fair comparison like this one is called a matched control.
Your design has to beat it on your own questions.
Otherwise you are only measuring the extra pieces.

slides.caption: A matched control gets the same number of pieces as the design under test. Without it, you measure the extra pieces instead of the idea.
slides.picture: A balance scale with the same number of plain pieces on one pan and shaped pieces on the other.

slides.title: Keyword search is *not optional*
slides.text: Run both kinds of search and merge the results.

narration: So far, search has worked by meaning, using vectors.
Search by meaning is poor at exact details, like a phone number.
Another kind of search looks for the exact text.
This is called keyword search.
In our tests on exact details, keyword search scored far higher.
Search by meaning does not show an error when it misses.
It returns something that looks right instead.
So run both kinds of search and merge the results.
It costs almost nothing.

slides.caption: On questions about an exact detail, keyword search scored far above search by meaning. A search by meaning that misses a phone number returns something that looks right.
slides.picture: A ring of nearly identical keys, and only one key fits the lock.

slides.title: More documents can mean *worse* answers
slides.text: Narrow the documents to the subject first.

narration: Now think about which documents belong in the search at all.
The whole set of documents that can be searched is called the corpus.
Adding more documents can make answers less accurate.
Published work showed accuracy coming back once the corpus was narrowed to the subject.
A few good documents usually work better than many.

slides.caption: Published work shows accuracy falling until the corpus was narrowed to the subject (arXiv 2606.11350). A few good documents usually beat many.
slides.picture: A large untidy pile of papers next to a small neat stack of three good documents beside a model device.

slides.title: Someone must *own* the corpus
slides.text: Responsibility for the corpus cannot be handed to software.

narration: Someone has to choose and tidy the documents in the corpus.
This can be done by people, by software with spot checks, or by both.
But one person or team must still own the corpus.
A real legal case shows why.
In Moffatt versus Air Canada, the company's chatbot went against its own policy.
The company was held responsible for what the chatbot said.

slides.caption: Moffatt v. Air Canada, BC Civil Resolution Tribunal, 14 February 2024. The company was held responsible for chatbot statements that went against its own policy.
slides.picture: A box file of documents with one blank owner tag tied to it, and a stamp beside it for spot checks.

slides.title: What an agent keeps is *memory*
slides.text: It reaches the model like any document.

narration: Documents are not the only thing the model sees.
An agent can also keep notes from its earlier work.
What it keeps is called memory.
When memory is used, it reaches the model just like a document.
So it needs the same care as a document.
It also brings some extra duties.

slides.caption: What an agent keeps from earlier work reaches the model like any document. It also carries duties a document does not.

slides.title: Memory is context that *lasts*

narration: Memory can last for different lengths of time.
Some lasts only for the current conversation.
Some lasts for a stretch of work of hours or days.
Both of these are ordinary engineering choices.
Memory kept after the work ends is different.
It becomes a record.
It needs someone who owns it.
It also needs consent to keep it.
And it needs rules for how long it is kept and when it is deleted.

slides.caption: The current conversation and hours or days of work are engineering choices. Memory kept after the work ends is a record with an owner, consent, and rules for keeping and deleting it.

slides.title: Four rules for what the agent *keeps*
items: Record when a fact was true

narration: Four rules follow from published evidence.
First, keep the original text.
Then add labels to help search find it.
In published tests, swapping the text for short facts or summaries made results worse.
Second, record when something happened.
Keep that apart from the time it was saved.
Then a fact that has been replaced can be marked out of date.
Third, check every new memory before it is kept.
It carries its source and waits for review.
In published work, planting bad entries in a tiny part of a memory store made most attacks succeed.
Fourth, topics are only labels that help search.
They are not the memory itself.
They can be rebuilt from the kept text.

slides.caption: Keep the source text, date each fact, check a memory before keeping it, and treat topics as labels. Sources: LongMemEval (ICLR 2025) and AgentPoison (NeurIPS 2024).

slides.title: The test for moving *on*

narration: So when is step two done?
There are three signs.
First, your way of splitting and storing documents beats a matched control.
It has to win on your own questions.
Second, everything the agent keeps has a source and a date.
It has also passed a check.
Third, the agent now finds the right facts.
What still goes wrong is what it does with them.

slides.caption: Move on when your design beats a matched control on your own questions. Kept memory must be sourced, dated and checked. What still fails should be about acting.

slides.title: Acting wrongly is a *step 3* problem

narration: Here is what that looks like.
The agent finds the right documents.
Then it draws the wrong conclusion, takes the wrong action, or stops too early.
That is not a context problem.
It belongs to step three, tools and the loop.

slides.caption: The agent finds the right documents. Then it draws the wrong conclusion, takes the wrong action or stops too early. That is a step 3 problem.

slides.title: What to *remember*
items: One vector can hide a topic

narration: Here is what to remember from step two.
A document is parsed, cut into chunks, turned into vectors, indexed and retrieved.
One vector for a document about many topics matches each topic only weakly.
Test any new design against a matched control on your own questions.
Run keyword search alongside search by meaning.
Give everything the agent keeps a source, a date and a check.
Next is step three, tools and the loop.

slides.caption: Documents are parsed, chunked, turned into vectors, indexed and retrieved. One vector hides topics. Beat a matched control. Use keyword search too. Check what the agent keeps.
